title: The First Exile to Babylon
overview: Judah's kings defy the rising empire of Babylon, and the result is a siege, a surrender, and the first large group of people carried off into exile.

parts.label: Rebellion and raiders (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Jehoiakim became a subject king paying tribute to Babylon, then broke away, and raiding bands from Babylon and neighboring peoples ravaged Judah. The writer reads this as the LORD's judgment, tied to the bloodshed of an earlier king, Manasseh, which is treated as guilt still resting on the nation.

parts.label: Jehoiakim dies, Egypt pulls back (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: Jehoiakim dies and his son takes the throne, though the prophet Jeremiah had warned he would not get an honorable burial, and how he died is not known. Babylon had pushed Egypt back to its own border, and some interpreters suggest Jehoiakim had rebelled hoping for Egyptian help, though the chapter does not say so.

parts.label: Jehoiachin's three months (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: The young king Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, ruled only three months. The writer judges him as following his father's path.

parts.label: Jerusalem surrenders (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: Babylon's army besieged the city, and when Nebuchadnezzar arrived in person, Jehoiachin gave himself up with his mother and court. Babylon's own records place the city's capture around 597 BC.

parts.label: Treasure and people taken (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: The temple and palace were stripped, which the writer sees as fulfilling the prophet Isaiah's earlier warning (2 Kings 20:17). Babylon took the leaders, soldiers and skilled workers so the city could not fight back, leaving the poorest behind, though how the numbers in verses 14 and 16 fit together is unclear.

parts.label: Zedekiah, a puppet king (vv. 17-20)
parts.note: Nebuchadnezzar put Jehoiachin's uncle on the throne and renamed him Zedekiah, a common way conquerors showed who was really in charge. Zedekiah also rebelled, setting up the final destruction told in the next chapter.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this chapter means God directly sent Babylon against Judah, or that the writer is reading a political catastrophe through faith as God letting the nation reap the results of its choices.
think: When disaster falls on a whole community, how do you weigh the choices of its leaders against forces no one could have controlled?
